newsitem.title: UK: Trans-Zambezi Industries to list in London in Jan.
newsitem.headline: Trans-Zambezi Industries to list in London in Jan.

text.p: Southern African conglomerate Trans-Zambezi Industries Ltd (TZI) is to seek a full listing on the London Stock Exchange in January, 1997, in addition to its current listing in Luxembourg.

CEO Hilary Duckworth said in an interview in London that TZI already had backing from blue-chip institutional investors from the UK, Europe and the U.S. and was now looking for a broader private investor base to improve liquidity.

The company started out three years ago capitalised at $3.0 million but was now at $110 million, with some 46 million ordinary shares in issue. Net profit to shareholders for the year to September 30, 1996 was $8.1 million.

"Luxembourg has served its purpose but for many investors there is a comfort factor in a London listing," said Duckworth. TZI Ltd is also acquiring partial listings on the Zimbabwe Stock Exchange and the Lusaka Stock Exchange in Zambia.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell is TZI's adviser and broker and led the most recent capital raising in August when 16.75 million shares were issues at $2.25/share.

The group operates three divisions across Zimbabwe, Zambia and Botswana -- financial services, food and distribution and industrial, accounting for 40 percent, 20 percent and 40 percent of profits respectively. It has no exposure to South Africa.
"This is a rapidly growing company with an excellent track record of over 20 percent growth in earnings per share in dividend terms," Duckworth said.

He said it was also very undervalued at around 7x earnings now, against 14x for the Harare Stock Exchange generally, 12x for the Zimbabwe Industrial index and 18x for Tobacco Sales Ltd (TSL), a comparable company.

TZI recently acquired Zimbabwe's Art Corporation and Mutare Board & Paper manufacturing firms and has announced it will move into horticultural exporting from Zambia and Zimbabwe to supermarket chains in the UK and elsewhere.
It controls 90 percent of the choice beef market in Zambia, and is hoping to pick up useful additions from the break-up and disposal of Britain's Lonrho holdings.

TZI will also "look carefully" at the list of proposed privatisations to be published by the Zimbabwe government in January and will be aiming to expand its financial services division in 1997 -- its Bard Discount House in Zimbabwe now manages over $200 million in local pension fund assets.

Asked about repatriation of profits for foreign investors, Duckworth said 100 percent of profits from dividends could be taken out. Investment prior to 1980 could not as yet be remitted but all profits from it could.

He said both Zambia and Zimbabwe had a promising economic outlook, with Zimbabwe's growth rate widely underestimated because its statistical base was last calculated in 1981, "missing out on the 17 years when new companies were starting up and growing fastest."

Zambia was rapidly opening up its lucrative mining industry and some $1.2 billion has been pledged for investment in its northern Copperbelt region in the next two years. "But the (Zambian) kwacha will get a rough ride -- we see another 25 percent drop in two years," Duckworth added.
